lead: Paul’s sermon reaches its heart: “God raised him from the dead”, and so fulfilled what he had promised to the ancestors, as the second psalm says: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” The same psalm is today’s responsorial psalm. In the Gospel, on the night before he dies, Jesus calms troubled hearts: he goes to prepare a place, and he himself is the way there. Today is the optional memorial of St George, martyr, and of St Adalbert, bishop and martyr.

r.h: God raised him from the dead
set: Paul turns from history to the present: “to us the message of this salvation has been sent.” Like the apostles throughout Acts, he tells the Passion briefly and lays the weight on the Resurrection and its witnesses. He speaks to fellow Jews and God-fearers as brothers, and he describes the condemnation of Jesus in Jerusalem as an act done without understanding, which God turned into the fulfilment of the prophets (compare 3:17).
str: vv. 26–29: the word sent to us; the Passion according to the Scriptures.
vv. 30–31: God raised him; the witnesses from Galilee.
vv. 32–33: the good news: the promise fulfilled; Psalm 2.
kw: Literally “not knowing”. Peter said the same in Jerusalem (3:17). The New Testament treats this ignorance as a real fault in those responsible, yet one that leaves room for repentance, and it never extends the guilt to all Jews of that time or of today (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).

Paul says Jesus was taken down from the “tree”, the word of Deuteronomy 21:22–23, where one hanged on a tree is under a curse. Peter uses it too (5:30; 10:39), and Paul explains it in Galatians 3:13: Christ became a curse for us.

In Psalm 2 the king of David’s line is declared God’s son on the day he is enthroned. The apostles see that “today” in the Resurrection: Jesus, eternally the Son, is now enthroned in power as Son in his risen humanity (Romans 1:4).
vv: Because the residents of Jerusalem and their leaders did not recognize him or understand the words of the prophets that are read every sabbath, they fulfilled those words by condemning him.
The irony is deliberate: the very prophets read aloud every sabbath were fulfilled by those who did not grasp them. The Church adds that all sinners are the authors of Christ’s Passion (CCC 598).
But God raised him from the dead;
One short verse carries the whole sermon. The verses before it tell what people did; this one tells what God did.
and they are now his witnesses to the people.
Paul does not count himself among those who came up from Galilee. He rests his preaching on the witnesses of the Easter appearances, as he does in 1 Corinthians 15:3–8.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Resurrection fulfils the promises of the Old Testament and of Jesus himself, and it joins Psalm 2 to the Resurrection as Paul does here (CCC 652–653). Each Sunday the Church gathers as Paul’s hearers did, to hear the Scriptures read and to be told that they are fulfilled in the risen Christ.

r.h: I am the way, and the truth, and the life
set: The supper is over and Jesus has foretold Peter’s denial (13:38). Into the disciples’ fear he speaks the first words of his long farewell. These words are often read at funerals, and rightly; but they were first spoken to men who were about to see their Master arrested and killed.
str: v. 1: “Do not let your hearts be troubled”: faith in God and in Jesus.
vv. 2–3: the Father’s house, a place prepared, a promise to come again.
vv. 4–6: Thomas’ question; “I am the way”.
kw: The same verb was used of Jesus himself, troubled in spirit before the betrayal (13:21). He does not ask from them a calm he has never known; he has passed through trouble and speaks from beyond it.
From the verb menō, to remain, a favorite word of John. The Father and the Son will make their “home” (monē) with whoever loves Jesus (14:23). Heaven begins as an indwelling now.
Not only a road to walk but a Person to walk with. The first Christians were called people “of the Way” (Acts 9:2).
vv: In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places.

Many rooms: room enough for all, and each person known. Earlier in John “my Father’s house” was the Temple (2:16); now it is the Father’s own presence, to which the risen body of Jesus, the true Temple, leads.
Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?
Thomas asks what the others only think. His honest question draws out one of the greatest sayings in the Gospel: a doubt spoken to Jesus becomes a door.
I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.
St Augustine puts it simply: walk by Christ the man and you come to Christ who is God; by him you go to him (in substance).
ch: The Church confesses with this verse that Christ is the one mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5). For troubled hearts the verse is first a comfort: the way home is not a set of directions but a Person who walks with us. The Easter season lets us hear it in the light of the empty tomb: he has gone ahead, and the place is ready.

qa: Does “No one comes to the Father except through me” mean that those who are not Christians cannot be saved?

All who are saved are saved through Christ. The Second Vatican Council teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel of Christ or his Church, yet seek God with a sincere heart and, moved by grace, try to do his will as they know it through conscience, can attain eternal salvation (Lumen Gentium 16; CCC 847). There is one way, and the grace of Christ reaches further than our knowledge of it. This is no reason to slacken the mission; it is the reason for it (CCC 848).
rite: St George, a soldier martyred probably at Lydda in Palestine early in the fourth century, is honored in East and West alike; the stories of the dragon came much later and teach in picture that faith overcomes evil. Many churches in Kerala bear his name. St Adalbert (Vojtěch), Bishop of Prague, was martyred in 997 while preaching to the Prussians near the Baltic coast. Both did what Paul describes today: they were witnesses of the risen Lord to the people, at the cost of their lives.
study: Which of my troubles do I need to bring to Jesus this week with Thomas’ honesty?
Where am I trying to reach the Father by my own road rather than walking with Christ, the Way?
